profiles.name: Personal & Professional Development
profiles.actualContent: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate student formation, namely, actively, consciously and ethically relating to oneself, others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhances critical thinking and independent learning. It also helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners. The course stimulates core academic skills, namely: Select and critically analyze academic sources Articulate research questions, thesis statements and arguments Improve communication skills through various forms of writing and speaking activities The course fosters personal, social and civic competencies, namely: Craft own academic and personal learning goals Critically reflect on own learning Develop effective collaborative learning approaches with peers, instructors and external partners Valuing community engagement, including the value of different knowledge types and perspectives
profiles.judgment: First-year academic writing, research questions, personal reflection and civic engagement; not the B3 linguistics professional think tank.

profiles.name: AI Ethics
profiles.actualContent: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation.
profiles.judgment: AI bias, privacy, agency, moral status and psychological/social implications; genuine ethics, not analysis of language structure or NLP methods.

profiles.name: Decision-making in AI
profiles.actualContent: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
profiles.judgment: Planning, uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints. Genuine AI content without a language-specific application sequence.

profiles.name: Optimization Methods in AI
profiles.actualContent: Artificial Intelligence is concerned with building intelligent machines that can compute how to act effectively and safely in a wide variety of novel situations. Computer agents operate autonomously, perceive their environment, persist over a prolonged time period, adapt to change, and create and pursue goals. A rational agent is one that acts so as to achieve the best expected outcome. This course aims to provide the student with foundational abilities in: searching in complex and adversarial environment and optimizing by rational agents. Topics include uninformed and informed search in discrete and completely known environments, local and global search methods in unknown and continuous environments, games played in adversarial environments and constraint satisfaction problems. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of experimental investigations into areas such as graph search, constraint satisfaction, convex optimization, linear and non-linear programming. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
profiles.judgment: Search, games, constraint satisfaction and optimisation with laboratory projects. Not computational linguistic modelling.

profiles.name: Reinforcement Learning
profiles.actualContent: Explores reinforcement learning. Covers theoretical frameworks and algorithms and requires students to implement algorithms and build agents using neural networks that learn through trial and error.
profiles.judgment: Reinforcement-learning theory and neural agents; no evidenced language acquisition or speech application.

profiles.name: Networks & Operating Systems
profiles.actualContent: Computer networks are the foundations on which the modern commercial, entertainment, industrial, and social world is built. An operating system (OS) is system software that is the interface between computer hardware and applications. The first part of the semester is organized around layers of a computer network architecture. The main focus is on the Internet, its architecture and protocols are used for studying fundamental concepts. The second half of the semester starts by introducing the typical structure of an OS, by distinguishing between processes and threads, and by explaining how an OS schedules work. Then consideration is given to the issues of concurrency, memory management, and file systems. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with how the Internet works and how the Internet can be monitored and controlled, moreover, a sound understanding of the pivotal role an OS plays in the managing of resources and the running of applications.
profiles.judgment: Internet protocols, processes, concurrency, memory and file systems; computing infrastructure, not language technology.

profiles.name: Database Management Systems
profiles.actualContent: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.
profiles.judgment: Relational theory, SQL, normalisation and query processing; data organisation, not corpus design or annotation.

profiles.name: Software Development
profiles.actualContent: Software development is designing, creating, testing, and maintaining software applications. We learn to program in C++, which offers fine-grained control over system resources, and in Haskell, which is a purely functional programming language. Various stages of software development such as planning and requirements gathering, testing and quality assurance, deployment and maintenance is covered in laboratory format consisting mostly on in-class discussions and code reviews. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of programming in C++ and in Haskell. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
profiles.judgment: C++/Haskell software design, testing and maintenance; no guaranteed linguistic software project.

profiles.name: Algorithms & Data Structures
profiles.actualContent: This course aims to provide the student with knowledge, skills and critical thinking ability in algorithm design and analysis. Inappropriate choice of algorithm and associated data structure can seriously impact on the performance of an application. The st udy of algorithm design and analysis provides techniques which help minimize the execution time of an algorithm. An emphasis is on the experimental performance analysis of algorithms. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Larger algorithm projects are also undertaken. There is a written midterm exam and a written final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained an understanding of how algorithms have helped shape the modern world.
profiles.judgment: Algorithm design, data structures and experimental performance analysis; generic computational foundation.

profiles.name: Advanced Algorithms
profiles.actualContent: The realm of Algorithms certainly needs further exploration beyond the standard topics of an Algorithms and Data Structures course. We study modern algebraic algorithms and solution methods for optimization problems. The course will provide you with the knowledge and experience of advanced computational techniques with emphasis on algorithmic thinking and mathematical modelling. The second meeting of the class each week is entirely devoted to laboratory work where students tackle exercises and demonstrate their work. Projects are undertaken to provide experience of experimental investigations into areas such as fast arithmetic, arbitrary precision and advanced optimization methods. There are written Midterm and Final exams.
profiles.judgment: Algebraic algorithms, optimisation and mathematical modelling; follows algorithmic foundation but not NLP specialisation.

profiles.name: Introduction to Data Science
profiles.actualContent: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question.
profiles.judgment: Data cleaning/visualisation includes text among several data types and a project. Genuine partial text-data contribution; not corpus linguistics.

profiles.name: Machine Learning
profiles.actualContent: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations.
profiles.judgment: Regression, classification, resampling, trees, SVM and clustering. General machine-learning methods, no dedicated language applications.

profiles.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
profiles.actualContent: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E).
profiles.judgment: Actual Python neural networks, text classification and LLMs alongside tabular/computer-vision applications. Direct partial language-technology content; do not count all 7.5 EC as NLP.

profiles.name: Introduction to Programming
profiles.actualContent: This is the gateway course of Computer Science and AI studies; an introductory course in problem solving and computer programming in Python. The course begins by introducing traditional structured programming and data constructs (i.e. branching, loops, functions; tuples and lists). Then consideration is given to testing and debugging and finally the object- oriented programming constructs. During the entire semester, elements of discrete mathematics (e.g., logic, sets, enumeration) as well as certain computational problem solving techniques are also incorporated into the course material. There are classes twice a week. The first half of each class is a lecture where we learn new material, while the second half is devoted to laboratory work where students tackle programming exercises and demonstrate their work. Homework comprises weekly programming exercises and online quizzes. Two larger programming projects are undertaken. There is a written Midterm exam and a written Final exam. By the end of the course a student will have obtained a reasonable familiarity with the Python programming language as well as important concepts of discrete mathematics and computational problem solving techniques.
profiles.judgment: Python, discrete mathematics, testing and programming projects. Genuine programming foundation, not language-specific programming.

profiles.name: Mathematical Methods
profiles.actualContent: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3
profiles.judgment: Calculus, complex numbers and differential equations with multidisciplinary applications. Generic quantitative foundation.

profiles.name: Linear Algebra
profiles.actualContent: Linear algebra is the study of systems of linear equations and linear functions. Systematic methods exist to solve such systems of linear equations. Matrices and vectors are introduced as the equivalent of a system of linear equations. This equivalence allows for reducing problems involving linear combinations of vectors to questions about systems of linear equations. The spanning of a (sub)space, linear independence and linear transformations are fundamental concepts in linear algebra. Matrix operations and theorems involving matrices will provide the basic tools for handling many applications of linear algebra. The invertible matrix theorem is a theorem of particular importance. The determinant of a matrix is an important scalar quantity related to the invertibility criterion for square matrices. Furthermore, the determinant is a measure for the amount by which a linear transformation changes the area of a ﬁgure. In multi-variable calculus, this measure is deﬁned as the Jacobian of a transformation. Introducing the more abstract concept of vector spaces allows for further generalization of these ideas. Many vector spaces resemble the well-known vector space Rn. In this course, the theory of vector spaces will be applied to the processing of discrete signals (Fourier Series), diﬀerence equations and Markov chains. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to understand the action of a linear transformation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors arise naturally in diﬀerent areas of physics and mathematics.
profiles.judgment: Vectors, matrices, spaces, transformations, Fourier series and Markov chains; foundation for modelling, not linguistic description.

profiles.name: Linear Systems
profiles.actualContent: The concepts of signals and systems appear in a wide variety of fields. The physical nature of the sig- nals to be acquired and the measurement systems may differ from application to application, but they all have in common that the signals contain information about the observed phenomenon and secondly, the systems respond to particular signals by producing other signals or certain behavior as output. This course discusses how to characterize alinear time-invariant systemand how it will respond to var- ious inputs. Theunit-impulse responseor - its equivalent in the frequency domain - thefrequency responsecharacterizes a linear time-invariant system. This course discussesconvolution. TheFourier series representationrepresents periodic signals as infinite harmonic series in continuous time and finite harmonic series in discrete time. Increasing the period of the periodic signals amounts to a denser Fourier series representation. In the limiting case that the period becomes infinitely long, the Fourier series rep- resentation becomes theFourier transform- both in continuous-time and in discrete-time. The course discusses the properties of the Fourier series representation and the Fourier transform in great detail. A very important characteristic of the Fourier transform is the duality property. TheLaplace transform generalizes the Fourier transform for continuous-time signals. In a very similar way, theZ-transform generalizes the Fourier transform for discrete-time signals.
profiles.judgment: Signals, convolution, Fourier/Laplace/Z transforms and linear systems. No actual speech-recognition or acoustic-phonetics curriculum is established.

profiles.name: Probability & Statistics
profiles.actualContent: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
profiles.judgment: Probability, distributions, estimation and simulation; general mathematical statistics, not language-data experimental practice.

profiles.name: Philosophy of Mind
profiles.actualContent: o What is the nature of consciousness? o What explains the identity of selves over time? How have different philosophical traditions thought about this issue? o Can the mind be explained in neurobiological terms? o Are large language models conscious? Can they ever be? o What can we learn from dream states about conscious experience? o What can perceptual illusions teach us about our awareness of the world? o What are the differences between human and animal consciousness? These are some of the questions explored in the philosophy of mind, an important field of philosophy since early modernity. The field has come to prominence and maturation in the past decades alongside advances in the scientific study of the human mind, research on animal minds, and innovations in computing. In this course, we will focus both on important work from the history of the field and on contributions from recent scholarship. We shall begin with exploration of the nature of selves and personal identity, looking at historical sources in the Western tradition, contemporary debate, as well as the theory of the self in Buddhist thought. Detailed discussion of approaches to the mind-body problem, a key issue in the philosophy of mind, will follow. Additional topics to be examined in the course include: the possibility of intelligent and conscious machines, animal minds, dream states, the significance of transformative experiences, and the impact of novel technologies on the ways we experience the world.
profiles.judgment: Consciousness, selves, mind-body problem and intelligent machines; cognitive context, not semantics/pragmatics theory.

profiles.name: Introduction to Sociology
profiles.actualContent: Sociology provides a diverse and intricate toolkit composed of concepts, methods, and theories, which aids in comprehending and dissecting the functioning of societies on a local scale and the complex interconnections triggering global phenomena. Unlike disciplines like economics or political science, the subject of sociological inquiry is less clearly de fined. It encompasses all facets of human engagement within society, spanning from everyday interactions to the most longstanding social institutions. As a result, the wealth of knowledge within sociology can feel daunting, leaving one uncertain about where to begin. The course follows the recommendations 3 of the Sociological Literacy Framework 1, which is composed of the essential concepts and competencies in the discipline, as portrayed in the following table: Furthermore, this course overviews some of the most impactful sociological theories, including those by Marx, Weber, Durkheim, and Du Bois. It recognizes the social and historical backdrop that shaped these “classical” sociological ideas and concepts, notably influenced by imperialism and colonialism. This historical context notably sidelined the voices of BIPOC (Black, Indigenous, and People of Color) and women. Consequently, fundamental concepts like race and gender received inadequate theoretical attention within “classical” sociology. To bridge this gap, the course will prioritize students ’ interests and intellectual needs.
profiles.judgment: Classical social theory, institutions, race/gender/class and social context. Not sociolinguistic variation, multilingual communities or conversation analysis.

profiles.name: Modern Sociology
profiles.actualContent: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
profiles.judgment: Modernity, imperialism, colonial responses and social theory; social context, not sociolinguistics.

profiles.name: Neurobiology
profiles.actualContent: Cognitive neuroscience uses inputs and perspectives from many disciplines, such as psychology, biology, medicine, computer science, and philosophy. In this course, the focus will be on the biology side of neuroscience. As a result, we will focus on evoluti onary pressures on animals in general, resulting in specific behaviors and physiological processes in these animals and ourselves. In this light, you will gain a greater understanding of biorhythms and natural behaviors, and eventually of specific disorders and diseases. Additionally, we will take a look at the use of animals in neuroscientific research, such as rodents, and discuss ethical and welfare implications. We will also familiarize you with experimental techniques in the laboratory, such as cell st aining and using a microscope, and compare the (brain) anatomy of different animal species. This course will familiarize you with concepts and skills required within the discipline of Neurobiology. A selected number of key topics within the field will be discussed, including comparative anatomy, biorhythms, animal models and ethics, and disorders . The course also includes guest lectures and practical work such as labwork, group assignments and student presentations.
profiles.judgment: Comparative neuroanatomy, animal models, biorhythms and laboratory techniques. Not speech, voice and hearing science.

profiles.name: Perception & Action
profiles.actualContent: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
profiles.judgment: Neural mechanisms of perception and goal-directed action; cognitive complement, not experimental speech analysis.

profiles.name: Higher Order Functions
profiles.actualContent: This course builds upon the knowledge gained in the introductory course in Cognitive Science. It will deepen your knowledge of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Also, your knowledge of experimental approaches in the field of cognitive neuroscience will be enhanced; such that you become able to evaluate research findings and to design your own experiments. A selected number of higher order cognitive processes will be dealt with, including memory, emotion, social cognition, attention, consciousness, decision making and planning. In addition to established knowledge, current research questions will be discussed in depth.
profiles.judgment: Memory, emotion, attention, social cognition, consciousness and experimental evaluation/design; general cognition, not another language course.

profiles.name: Psycholinguistics
profiles.actualContent: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
profiles.judgment: Direct psycholinguistics: neuroscience of language, speech production/comprehension, aphasia, acquisition, bilingualism, semantics, reading/dyslexia and experiments. Strong 7.5 EC contribution, without a cumulative formal-linguistics sequence.

profiles.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
profiles.actualContent: This 100-level course ‘Introduction to Brain & Behavior’ constitutes the Gateway Course for the Cluster Health, Cognition and Behavior: Units ‘Cognitive Science’ and ‘Clinical Psychology’. In this course you will gain foundational knowledge and essential skills that you will need in intermediate and advanced courses of these units. We will look at the various ways in which psychologists and neuroscientists have approached questions such as: Why do people behave the way they do? Can we predict behavior and mental processes in a particular situation, for example after brain damage? Is it possible to change these behaviors and mental processes? How do nature and nurture interact in the development of how we think, feel and behave? Which areas of the brain serve which function, and how do neurons communicate with each other and with the body? We will explore these complex and fascinating topics together from a neuroscientific and psychological perspective, learning about functional brain anatomy on a micro and macro scale, research methodologies and tools in the fields of Cognitive Science and Clinical Psychology, as well as main psychological theories and the relevance of main clinical skills in Psychology. The course will be organized including a combination of different methods of teaching and learning; e.g. interactive lectures, individual and team activities with a collaborative learning methodology, guest lectures, reflective activities, among others. Course outline HCBGATE102 Introduction to Brain & Behavior Page 2 of 16
profiles.judgment: Brain/behaviour, neuroanatomy, psychology and research tools; coherent gateway for psycholinguistics, not language-science introduction.

profiles.name: Social Psychology
profiles.actualContent: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
profiles.judgment: Scientific social psychology of influence and interpersonal behaviour. Not conversation analysis or language variation.

profiles.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
profiles.actualContent: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in in medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers whether in data science, business analytics, market research, political science or sociology. The phenomena investigated by scientists studying humans are usually complex, thus multiple variables must be used to explain them. The theory and application of multivariate statistical models will be discussed. These models can be used to investigate the relations among many variables simultaneously, thus providing an accurate explanation of the subject of interest. The course introduces most used multivariate statistical models such as linear regression, factor analysis, analysis of (co)variance, and logistic regression. Furthermore, attention is paid to non-parametric tests. Practical application: you will learn to apply these models to data. In addition, learn how to deal with problems that occur when statistical models are used. At the end of the course, you will be able to determine which statistical model should be used to investigate different types of research questions. Furthermore, you will be able to execute the corresponding analyses and report results, conforming to APA guidelines.
profiles.judgment: Multivariate regression, factor analysis, AN(C)OVA, logistic/nonparametric analysis and APA reporting; relevant general methods, not successive linguistic research projects.

profiles.name: Advanced Research Seminar
profiles.actualContent: This course will introduce you to methods to perform systematic reviews and meta-analysis: the statistical analyses that are used to synthesize summary data from multiple of studies. Meta-analysis and systematic reviews are being used in many disciplines, including psychology, medicine, education, and others. Meta-Analysis and systematic reviews are very important tools in evidence based policy making as they allow to combine results of existing studies fairly objectively, to establish general treatment effect (effect size) and degree to which effect size is robust and consistent across the kinds of studies sampled. Participants will get hands-on experience in performing analyses using R. R is leading language in statistical computing. R is an open source language with huge number of individual and institutional users. The introduction to will help you the understand basics of R: program interface, syntax, variables and operations, reading data into R, accessing R packages, how to handle data structures, and create own functions. You will get acquainted with community developed packages providing common statistical analyses and practice conducting meta-analysis using R. The course is active learning oriented, with you presenting and performing preforming tasks in the class. As it is a 300 level course you are expected to take the responsibility for your learning and proactive attitude: come prepared to the class, complete homework/practice exercise and actively search answers to your questions and unclarified issues.
profiles.judgment: Systematic reviews and meta-analysis in R; evidence synthesis, not independent primary language-data collection or linguistics thesis.

profiles.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
profiles.actualContent: How do we become unique individuals? Which factors influence this process and how do they interplay in each stage of our development during our lives? In this course we will explore these and many other questions about human development, where students will acquire knowledge and develop critical thinking and understanding of the main aspects related to human development throughout the lifespan. The main goal of the course Developmental Psychology is to introduce the student to the basic concepts, issues and me thods in the field, which is concerned with human physical, cognitive, social and emotional development throughout the lifespan: from pregnancy to infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood and older age; their descriptions and understandings, as well as t he most relevant theoretical approaches and some psychological assessment and interventions in the different phases of life. Therefore, this course will address the following subject areas: 1. Historical and contemporary views, and main theories in Developmental Psychology; 2. Biological and environmental foundations of human development; 3. Pre-natal development and birth; 4. Attachment and physical, cognitive, emotional and social development in infancy. 5. Physical, cognitive, social, emotional and personality development in early and middle childhood, adolescence and early, middle and late adulthood; 6. End of life: death, dying, and bereavement.
profiles.judgment: Physical, cognitive, social and emotional development across the lifespan; not dedicated first/second-language acquisition or language-development disorders.

profiles.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
profiles.actualContent: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e.
profiles.judgment: Classical rhetorical argument and persuasive writing/speaking; relevant communication, not formal linguistic reasoning or structural analysis.

profiles.name: Style & Meaning
profiles.actualContent: The Style and Meaning course is firmly grounded in stylistics, which is the study of style in texts. Stylistics involves identifying and analysing the linguistic choices that serve to create meaning in texts. Originally an outgrowth of the third canon of classical rhetoric (elocutio), and later heavily influenced by movements in twentieth and twenty-first century linguistics, modern stylistics has grown into a recognizable discipline in its own right, with its own distinct theories and practices. While stylistics can be used to analyse any type of text, traditionally the discipline has been most concerned with the style of literary texts. As such, stylistics has sometimes been referred to as ‘literary stylistics’ or ‘literary linguistics.’ The course textbook also works almost exclusively with fictional texts to introduce and illustrate theoretical concepts and frameworks and their application. Nonetheless, further in-class application will at times extend beyond the fictional and students will be allowed to choose non-fictional texts for their instruction presentations and term papers. Students will be invited to consider the linguistic choices made by (literary) writers by reflecting on why certain linguistic strategies may be more effective than others in achieving particular interpretive effects. Students will be asked to consider all levels of language from the phonetic to the discoursal, to the cognitive. Therefore, an interest in language is crucial to this course.
profiles.judgment: Direct literary stylistics, linguistic choices at phonetic-to-discourse/cognitive levels, interpretive effects and textual analysis. Genuine 7.5 EC language contribution, not full phonetics/morphology/syntax/semantics.

profiles.name: Rhetoric in Action
profiles.actualContent: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed.
profiles.judgment: Rhetoric/community engagement and public-speaking teaching with primary pupils aged 9–12, drawing on introductory rhetoric. Not Dutch second-language pedagogy or language-disorder intervention.

profiles.name: Persuasive Communication
profiles.actualContent: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have.
profiles.judgment: Framing, nudging, persuasion, ethics and community communication problems. Builds on rhetoric; communication study rather than linguistic research.

profiles.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
profiles.actualContent: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material.
profiles.judgment: Poetry, performance, rhythm, sound and creative meaning-making. Genuine language-art contribution, not descriptive linguistics.

profiles.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
profiles.actualContent: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work.
profiles.judgment: Literary genres, practical criticism and interpretation. Textual complement, not grammar or corpus methods.

profiles.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
profiles.actualContent: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.
profiles.judgment: Humanist/feminist/Marxist/minority/psychoanalytic interpretive frameworks and text project. Not linguistic empirical research.

profiles.name: Introduction to Film & Media
profiles.actualContent: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media.
profiles.judgment: Film history, form, sound, narrative and political contexts. Not language structure or language processing.

profiles.name: Media Archaeology
profiles.actualContent: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts.
profiles.judgment: Material pre-digital media, memory and communication history; no language-science method or corpus substitution.

profiles.name: From T.V. to TikTok
profiles.actualContent: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves.
profiles.judgment: American social history and representation through TV/digital media; social communication context, not sociolinguistics.

weightedAssessment: Both original routes devote 15 EC to Psycholinguistics and Style & Meaning, genuine direct language study with different approaches. Primary: 37.5 EC communication/rhetoric/creative-language courses (including stylistics), 37.5 EC neuroscience, 30 EC psychology/statistics/meta-analysis/development, 15 EC sociology, 15 EC literature, 22.5 EC media, 7.5 EC philosophy, 7.5 EC data science and 7.5 EC PPD =180. The computational route has 127.5 EC computing/AI/data/mathematics, 37.5 EC brain/neurobiology/higher cognition/psycholinguistics/psychology methods, 7.5 EC stylistics and 7.5 EC PPD. Deep learning genuinely includes text classification/LLMs, but is broader than language. These partial strengths do not form a sustained descriptive/theoretical linguistic sequence or cumulative linguistic methods; general social theory is not sociolinguistics and signal processing is not speech science. Weighting is a substantive judgment, not a course-match quota.
boundedReconstruction: All40proposed profiles and actual-workbook scan for linguistic structure/acquisition/methods inspected. Only psycholinguistics and stylistics directly sustain linguistics; creative language and text/LLM computing add partial contributions. Film syntax, image morphology and generic signals are not language-science replacements. No evidence-backed complete reconstruction established. Sound partial content and formal placement checks preserved; active alternatives withdrawn.
